problem: Existing social navigation platforms are tied to specific planner types, use oversimplified human behavior models (widening the sim2real gap), rely on a single simulator, and offer little environment randomization or planner diversity.
motivation: Robots in healthcare, logistics and delivery must navigate human-centric, crowded spaces, which requires realistic human-human and human-robot interaction simulation and rigorous, reproducible benchmarking. Prior Arena versions lacked realistic crowd models, social metrics and full simulator abstraction.
key_idea: Arena 3.0 is a ROS-based social navigation platform that abstracts core functions across Flatland, Gazebo and Unity, adding many social force models, social states, dynamic human-centric world generation, a benchmark task mode, social metrics and an extended MBF planner suite.
insight: The paper is a systems and benchmarking contribution, not a learning method. Its lesson is that unified abstraction across simulators plus social metrics exposes trade-offs among planners: LfLH is more socially compliant but less efficient, while the efficiency-trained Rosnav RL planner spends longer in pedestrians' private zones (avg 5.6 s). The user study (30 participants) gives qualitative evidence of improved usability, but it may be biased since 14 of the 30 had used earlier versions.
method: Arena-core simulator abstraction: unified core that runs task, world and pedestrian functions across Flatland (2D training), Gazebo (realistic kinematics) and Unity (photorealistic, RGB-D); LiDAR works in all three, RGB-D only in Gazebo and Unity

Human crowd modeling: integrates 9 social force models (Pedsim, PySocialForce as default, Deep Social, Evacuation, Bonding, ORCA, RVO2, etc.), with fixes for PySocialForce (group members follow a random group-leader waypoint; tolerant waypoint threshold to avoid spinning)
Pedsim Waypoint Plugin API: event-driven feedback loop that forwards Pedsim output to a plugin node and returns forces, so users can plug in custom SFMs
Social states and semantic layers: HHI/HRI/HOI states (talking, texting, avoiding or approaching the robot) plus a costmap Semantic Layer Plugin that stores pedestrian semantics for observation

Robot and planner suite on Move Base Flex: MBF navigation with an interplanner between global planner and local controller; ~18 planners (DWA, TEB, MPC, CoHAN, LfLH, SARL, CrowdNav, etc.) and 3 heuristic planners (aggressive, polite, sideways)
Task and world generator: random, scenario, guided, staged and benchmark task modes; 7 procedural map/world generators (Barn, Rosmap indoor/outdoor, Rosnav outdoor/canteen/industrial hall/office)
Social metrics and Arena-Web-v2: new metrics for time in private zone (0.5 m), time facing pedestrians and time seen by pedestrians; extended web companion app

setting.backbone: none (platform; benchmarked planners include DWA, TEB, MPC, LfLH, RLCA, Rosnav RL, etc.)
setting.training_data: none (simulation/benchmark platform; provides training pipeline for DRL agents)
setting.observation: 2D LiDAR (all simulators), RGB-D (Gazebo/Unity), semantic pedestrian layers
setting.action_space: continuous velocity commands for holonomic, differential-drive, car-like and quadruped robots

numbers_note: No tables of results; the planner benchmark (Jackal, 100 random episodes plus 10 per special environment) is shown only in figures; the only quoted number is the Rosnav average private-zone time of 5.6 s. The quantitative table in the source is commented out.
results: Arena 3.0 ran a benchmark with a Jackal robot on 100 random episodes (up to 30 pedestrians) plus 10 episodes each in canteen, industrial hall, office and corridor scenarios. LfLH was best on social metrics but less efficient, while Rosnav was efficient but spent 5.6 s on average in the private zone. A 30-participant user study reported improved installation, task generator robustness and planner variety versus earlier versions.
limitations: Requires Ubuntu 20.04 / ROS 1, with a learning curve and limited documentation for the API and Unity; a major API change hurt users of earlier versions
The benchmark is only demonstrated qualitatively through plots, without full quantitative tables; the user study is potentially biased (14 of 30 previous users)
Human behavior is still simulated by social force models with limited human-object interaction, and there is no real-robot validation
